rows.reply:
I hear you’re having trouble with the picture, so let’s read it together.

- The grey arrows point to the two axes: the horizontal axis is labelled **strain ΔL/L** (bottom right) and the vertical axis is labelled **stress F/A** (top left). 
- The straight blue line in the lower‑left part has the note **slope = E**; this means that in this region stress is proportional to strain, and the proportionality constant is the material’s Young’s modulus E. 
- The purple marker labeled **elastic limit** marks the end of that straight‑line region; up to this point the material will return to its original shape when the load is removed. 
- Beyond the elastic limit the red curve is labelled **plastic**; here the material deforms permanently even though the load keeps increasing. 
- At the far right the green point says **breaks**; this is where the material can no longer sustain the load and it fractures.

Overall, the graph shows how a metal’s stress (force per area) increases with strain (fractional stretch), first linearly (elastic behavior) and then non‑linearly (plastic deformation) until it finally breaks.

rows.said: what does the slope of the graph mean?
rows.reply:
The straight‑line part of the graph is the **elastic region**. Its slope tells you how quickly the stress ( force ÷ area ) rises as the strain ( change in length ÷ original length ) increases. That slope is called **Young’s modulus** — the material’s intrinsic “stiffness”. In symbols, 

\(E = \dfrac{\text{stress}}{\text{strain}}\) (Young’s modulus = stress divided by strain).

Now look at the **blue straight line** on the figure (the part labelled “slope = E”). 
**What do you notice about that line compared with the rest of the curve?**
